title: React Built-in Hooks vs Additional Hooks: What’s the Difference?
description: Confused about the difference between React Built-in Hooks vs Additional Hooks? Learn what they are, when to use them, and how to write better code.

blocks.v: React hooks revolutionized how we write components by enabling function components to manage state, side effects, refs, and more, without classes.

If you’ve used useState or useEffect, you’ve already seen the power of hooks. But React offers more than just these basic tools. There’s a distinction between built-in hooks (used daily) and additional or advanced hooks (used for performance, dev tools, or fine control).
Understanding the difference is key to writing clean, optimized, and scalable React code.

v: Best practices for choosing the right hook

blocks.v: React hooks are special functions that let you hook into React features (like state and lifecycle methods) from function components. They start with use, and they only work inside function components or custom hooks.
Built-in hooks are the essential hooks every React developer uses regularly. They ship with React and are used to manage common needs like state, side effects, and performance.
Reference DOM elements or persist values

v: Interacting with external systems (e.g. APIs, storage)

blocks.v: React also provides a few less commonly used hooks that are considered "advanced" or "additional." These are designed for more complex scenarios, like fine-tuning performance, working with layout or animations, or customizing how refs behave.
Shows custom labels in React DevTools
Exposes custom instance values for ref
Defers updating a value for better responsiveness
Generates unique IDs for accessibility and hydration
Injects styles before DOM mutations (advanced use case)

v: Needing developer tooling or ref control

blocks.v: When to Use Built-in vs Additional Hooks

head: Built-in hooks
Additional hooks
rows: After you have measured, or when the pattern genuinely fits

blocks.v: The common mistake is treating the second column as a sign of seniority and wrapping everything in useMemo and useCallback. Both have a cost of their own, and applied everywhere they usually make a component slower and always make it harder to read.
Don't reach for useLayoutEffect or useImperativeHandle unless necessary. They add complexity and are harder to maintain.
useContext is great for low-frequency global state (like theme or auth), but not for fast-updating values like typing or animations.
Failing to memoize can cause unnecessary re-renders in performance-sensitive areas.
Best Practices for Using React Hooks

v: Use built-in hooks for 90% of your needs
Use additional hooks only when performance or layout control is needed
Write custom hooks to encapsulate logic and avoid repetition
Memoize functions/values when props are passed deeply
Keep each hook focused on a single concern

blocks.v: Summary: Know Which Hook to Reach For
React hooks are powerful tools, but knowing when and which one to use makes the difference between code that just works and code that scales.
You don’t need to memorize all the hooks. Just understand their purpose and use them when the problem calls for it.
